impact.location_description: Above Normandy, France, near Angiens/Saint-Pierre-le-Viger, Seine-Maritime; fragmented at ~28 km altitude
impact.context: Populated rural region of northern France, night sky, widely witnessed and captured by the dedicated FRIPON all-sky camera network, only ~7 hours after discovery, prompting a rapid public mobilization.

meteorites.name: Saint-Pierre-le-Viger
meteorites.class: L5-6 ordinary chondrite breccia, shock stage S3
meteorites.notes: Recovered by the FRIPON/Vigie-Ciel citizen-science network; first ~100 g stone found within 2 days of the fall, eventually >60 stones totaling just over 1 kg. Fell 220 years (almost to the location) after the historic 1803 L'Aigle fall in the same region of Normandy, itself an L6 breccia.

confirmation.eyewitness: Thousands of witnesses across northern France and southern England reported the fireball; extensive video record.

scientific_results: First 'targeted' meteor observation in history: because the impact corridor was known hours in advance, FRIPON/Vigie-Ciel could alert its camera network and the public in real time rather than relying on chance coverage.

One of only two cases (with 2008 TC3) where both accurate pre-impact astrometric/photometric data and a full multi-station atmospheric-entry trajectory and dark-flight/strewn-field model exist for the same recovered meteorite, letting researchers connect telescope-based size/rotation estimates directly to entry dynamics and lab meteorite properties.

Egal et al. 2025 (Nature Astronomy) present a complete, closed-loop characterization: pre-atmospheric orbit and rotation state from telescopic photometry, catastrophic disruption dynamics from camera-network light curves (fragmentation at ~4 MPa dynamic pressure, ~98% of kinetic energy released in a narrow altitude band near 28 km), and petrology/mineralogy of the recovered L5-6 breccia, used together as a test case for planetary-defense airburst modeling of meter-scale stony impactors.

Shock stage S3 and brecciated texture in Saint-Pierre-le-Viger stones tie the source body to a moderately shocked L-chondrite parent, adding one more data point (alongside Almahata Sitta and Ribbeck) to the small but growing sample of meter-scale NEOs with both known pre-impact orbits and known meteorite classes.

notable_papers.topic: Recovery and planned study of the Saint-Pierre-le-Viger meteorite

narrative: Hungarian astronomer Krisztián Sárneczky, working alone at the Piszkéstető Schmidt telescope in the Mátra Mountains, picked up a faint moving object on the evening of 12 February 2023; within hours the Minor Planet Center's automated systems flagged it as an imminent impactor headed for northern France. With just under seven hours of warning, the FRIPON/Vigie-Ciel network — built precisely for this kind of rapid response — alerted its dedicated all-sky camera stations across France and mobilized public spotters. The object, 2023 CX1, streaked in at 02:59 UTC on 13 February, fragmenting catastrophically around 28 km altitude in a blaze visible across Normandy and southern England. Search teams recovered the first meteorite fragment, later named Saint-Pierre-le-Viger, within two days, eventually gathering more than sixty stones a little over a kilometer from where L'Aigle's historic 1803 meteorite fall had struck the same corner of Normandy 220 years earlier. The combination of pre-impact telescopic data, a dense multi-camera atmospheric trajectory, and laboratory analysis of recovered stones made 2023 CX1 one of the most completely characterized small-asteroid falls ever studied, published as a landmark Nature Astronomy paper in 2025.
